constraints: All values in nums are distinct.
nums is sorted in increasing order.

examples.explain: 5 would sit between 2 and 7, but it isn't there.

followUp: If nums could contain duplicates, how would you return the first index of target?
hints: A scan works but ignores the sorting. If you look at the middle value and it's too small, what do you know about everything to its left?
Keep two indices lo and hi so that the target, if present, is always somewhere in nums[lo..hi].
Probe mid = (lo + hi) // 2. Too small: lo = mid + 1. Too big: hi = mid - 1. Stop when lo > hi.

insight.mnemonic: Guess the middle page of the dictionary, then tear the wrong half off.
insight.oneLiner: Probe the middle; sortedness tells you which half can't contain the target, so throw it away.

recall.a: If the target exists, it lies in nums[lo..hi]. The loop runs while that range is non-empty (lo ≤ hi).
recall.q: What is the loop invariant of iterative binary search?

recall.a: nums[mid] was already checked. Keeping it can leave lo == hi == mid forever - an infinite loop.
recall.q: Why lo = mid + 1 rather than lo = mid?

recall.a: With an inclusive range, lo == hi is one unchecked candidate. lo < hi would exit without checking it.
recall.q: Why while lo <= hi and not lo < hi?

signals: find a value or its position
insight.why: In a sorted array, nums[mid] < target means every index ≤ mid is also too small. One comparison eliminates half the candidates, so n candidates run out after about log₂ n probes.

oneLiner: Probe the middle; sortedness tells you which half can't contain the target, so throw it away.

pitfalls.explain: You returned -1 for a target that is in the array. With an inclusive range, `while lo < hi` exits while one candidate (lo == hi) is still unchecked - use `while lo <= hi`.
pitfalls.title: Stopped one candidate too early

pitfalls.explain: The target isn't in the array, but you returned an index. Return -1 when the range runs out, and only return mid after nums[mid] == target.
pitfalls.title: Returned an index for a missing target

pitfalls.explain: Setting lo = mid (or hi = mid) keeps an already-checked index in the range. Once lo and hi are adjacent or equal, mid never changes and the loop never ends. Use mid + 1 and mid - 1.
pitfalls.title: The range stopped shrinking

solutions.idea: Check every value in order. Correct, but it reads up to n values and ignores the one thing the problem gives you: the array is sorted.
solutions.name: Linear scan

footnotes.text: Name the invariant before writing the loop: "if target exists, it is in nums[lo..hi]". Every update below must keep that sentence true.
One comparison rules out half the range, not just one element. That's the whole algorithm: sortedness turns each probe into a verdict on an entire side.
mid - 1, not mid: nums[mid] was already checked. Keeping mid in the range would let lo == hi == mid loop forever.

solutions.idea: Keep the target's possible range as [lo, hi]. Each probe of the middle either finds it or halves the range, so about log₂ n probes decide the answer.
solutions.name: Iterative binary search

starter:
class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
statement:
You're given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers sorted in increasing order, and an integer `target`. Return the index where `target` appears, or `-1` if it isn't in the array.

Your solution should run in **O(log n)** time - fast enough that it never needs to look at most of the array.
title: Binary Search
